children: The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economy is projected to contract by 4.8% in 2026 before rebounding with growth of 9.1% in 2027, as disruptions to energy production and trade weigh heavily on regional economic activity, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Regional Economic Outlook: Middle East and Central Asia, has sharply downgraded its 2026 growth forecast for the six GCC economies from 2% projected in April, while raising its 2027 forecast from 4.8%. Oman is the only GCC country expected to record economic growth in 2026, with its gross domestic product (GDP) projected to expand by 4.1%, the report said.

The outlook reflects the uneven economic impact of the Middle East conflict, which has disrupted hydrocarbon production, energy exports, shipping, tourism and trade. The IMF expects a substantial recovery in 2027 as energy production and trade gradually normalise.

Among the GCC economies, Kuwait is projected to record the steepest contraction in 2026, with GDP declining by 16.7%, followed by Qatar at 15.6% and Bahrain at 11.3%. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are forecast to contract by 3.3% and 3.9%, respectively.

Oman’s economy is projected to grow by 4.1% in 2026, although the IMF expects the sultanate’s growth to moderate to 2.2% in 2027. The country’s relatively limited exposure to disruptions associated with the Strait of Hormuz has helped support its economic outlook, according to the report.

The IMF expects a strong rebound across the GCC in 2027, led by Qatar, where GDP is projected to grow by 18.8%, followed by Kuwait at 17.1% and Bahrain at 13.9%. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are forecast to expand by 7.9% and 7.7%, respectively.

The projected recovery is based on the IMF’s baseline assumption that hostilities will ease and energy production and trade conditions will gradually return to normal by the end of 2027. The report assumes disruptions to energy trade and production will continue through the first quarter of 2027, followed by a gradual recovery in flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Inflation across the GCC is projected to rise in 2026 before easing moderately in 2027, as higher food, energy and transportation costs feed through to consumer prices.

The IMF expects average inflation across the six GCC economies to increase to 2.7% in 2026, from 0.9% in 2025, before easing to 2.4% in 2027. Inflation is projected to return to 2% from 2028, supported by lower commodity prices, exchange rate pegs and continued fiscal discipline.

The 2026 and 2027 inflation projections are slightly higher than those published in the IMF’s April outlook, reflecting the impact of higher commodity and transportation costs associated with the regional conflict.

The IMF’s report also highlights the risks to the outlook from further disruptions to energy production and trade routes. Such disruptions could push energy prices further higher, weaken economic growth and intensify inflationary pressures.
